output.headline: EU, UK and developing nations march on Cop31 to save fossil fuel pledge
output.bodyHtml:
The EU, the UK, many African countries and the world’s least developed and small island states marched on the Cop31 summit’s presidency office in Turkey on Saturday evening to demand the reinstatement of language committing to a transition away from fossil fuels, as the UK’s energy minister, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said discussions remained productive and “there is a deal to be done”.

The push came as the fortnight-long talks reached a standstill, with some countries mulling whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies, who have resisted calls to commit to phasing out fossil fuels.

The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress.

The key sticking points concerned the insistence by a loose coalition of about 130 countries on including a reference to the “transition away from fossil fuels” in the final outcome of the talks, as well as demands by developing countries to bolster their rights to funding from the rich world to help them adapt to the escalating impacts of the climate crisis. Saudi Arabia and some other oil-rich nations have consistently opposed an explicit statement on fossil fuel use.

A third draft of a potential headline agreement, released in the early hours on Sunday, attempted to address the impasse by saying countries recalled a deal reached in Dubai three years ago – the only summit at which countries have reached consensus on the need to move away from burning coal, oil and gas.

Maina Talia, climate minister for the low-lying Pacific island Tuvalu, said: “This [inclusion of a reference to fossil fuels] is a red line for us. We’re talking about the root cause of all this. [Without it] we are wasting our time here.”

Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, said: “We came to Antalya needing progress on public climate finance, adaptation and fossil fuels. Instead, we are fighting to stop governments retreating from promises they have already made. Rich countries have spent two weeks finding reasons not to deliver the [financial] support they promised. It feels like this meeting is unravelling.”

There were also strong disagreements over controversial “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology and a target to derive 35% of the world’s energy from electricity by 2035. Saudi Arabia wants strong recommendations of CCS in the final outcome from the talks, known as a “cover decision”, but other countries object as this technology is seen by some as a way to perpetuate the fossil fuel industry.

The third draft of the cover decision attempted to navigate this by removing a hard target for CCS and acknowledging that as much electrification as possible must be powered by clean energy. It was due to be debated at a formal session in the plenary hall scheduled for 9am local time.

Campaigners laid the blame for the lack of progress on the fossil fuel industry and the countries dependent on it, and on rich countries’ failure to deliver on promises of finance for poorer countries. “This must be the last time we allow fossil fuel interests, which are profiting so handsomely from the climate crisis, to hold us to ransom,” said Nick Dearden, director of the campaign group Global Justice Now. “It is abundantly clear by now that we will not be able to combat climate change as long as those who control the global economy can make money from coal, oil and gas.”

Harjeet Singh, global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign, said: “You can’t ask developing countries to transform their economies while they’re drowning in disasters and debt. Whatever deal emerges in Antalya, the world should know why this Cop failed. It wasn’t a lack of solutions, it was a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis.”

It was unclear when the talks, which were scheduled to end on Friday evening, would finish. Many delegates were rescheduling their flights home. If enough delegates leave, the “conference of the parties” (Cop) may no longer meet the quorum required under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.

The “transition away from fossil fuels” was agreed at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, but Saudi Arabia and its allies prevented further progress on putting it into action. At last year’s Cop30 the Brazilian hosts got around this by pledging to draft a global roadmap on the phaseout of fossil fuels.

This year the resolution appeared in a first draft of the agreed outcome from these talkswas excised from a revised draft published on Thursday, and was acknowledged obliquely in the third draft through a reference recalling the entire “United Arab Emirates consensus” reached in Dubai three years ago.

That inclusion came after the EU, the UK, many African countries and the world’s least developed countries, the small island states which are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis joined together on Saturday evening to march to the presidency office and demand reinstatement of the reference.

This is the first Cop with a dual presidency, owing to a compromise forged last year after both Australia and Turkey bid to host. Claudio Angelo, of the Observatorio do Clima, said this was part of the problem. “It goes to show how a weak presidency, split between two countries with little tradition in climate diplomacy, can be detrimental to a process already victimised by geopolitics,” he said.

One possible next step – which the Guardian understands to be under active consideration on Saturday night – could be to force an open meeting at which Saudi Arabia and any allies would be forced to publicly state their opposition to the stronger outcome that most other countries want.

This would be risky, as it could mean the collapse of the talks. But Bill Hare, chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank and a Cop veteran, told the Guardian: “If the overwhelming number of countries here want a strong text referencing the transition away from fossil fuels and so on and Saudi Arabia is on its own, I think Saudi Arabia will probably not stand against the global consensus.”

The Guardian also understands that China and India, though not allied with the “progressive coalition” of about 130 countries, are unlikely to stand against a deal.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK’s energy minister, said: “We are working closely with partners to find a way through and secure an agreement that moves us forward. These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done.”
output.standfirst: Climate talks in Antalya stalled as Saudi Arabia resisted a fossil fuel phase-out pledge, but the EU, UK and many developing and island nations marched on the summit presidency to demand its reinstatement.
output.progress: The UK's climate minister says talks remain productive, and analysts believe Saudi Arabia is unlikely to block the wider global consensus alone.

output.headline: Bradford councillor stable after stepping in to protect council worker
output.bodyHtml:
A statement on behalf of Ibrar Ali and his family, shared on Friday, said he had been supporting council wardens with community clean-up activities when he was attacked and stabbed.

They said: “During the incident, councillor Ibrar intervened to protect a member of council staff and, in doing so, sustained multiple stab wounds.”

The family said the councillor’s injuries were serious but not life-threatening, and that he was in a stable condition in hospital, adding that he was “grateful for the overwhelming kindness shown and hopes to personally thank everyone once he has recovered”.

A man has been charged with attempted murder, police said, after a local councillor was stabbed while working in the community in Bradford.

Arfan Ali, 32, is accused of attacking Ibrar Ali, 52, at about 11am on Thursday in the West Yorkshire city.

The alleged attacker has also been charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place, West Yorkshire police said.

He appeared at Leeds magistrates court on Saturday, the Crown Prosecution Service confirmed. He was reportedly remanded in custody ahead of his next appearance, at Bradford crown court on 21 December.

Officers were called just after 11am on Thursday to reports the councillor had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.

He is believed to have been injured first in Thornbury Avenue before being driven to Manse Street, according to the force.

Emergency services attended and took him to hospital.
output.standfirst: Ibrar Ali, 52, intervened to protect a member of council staff during an attack in Bradford, sustaining multiple stab wounds; he is in a stable condition, and Arfan Ali, 32, has been charged with attempted murder, assault and possessing an offensive weapon.
output.progress: Police have charged a man with attempted murder, assault and possessing an offensive weapon; he appeared in court on Saturday and is due back on 21 December.

output.headline: Suffolk MP speaks up for asylum seekers amid village's break-away vote
output.bodyHtml:
Suffolk MP Dr Peter Prinsley has hit back at opponents of asylum seekers who have described them as “illegals, criminals, rapists”, insisting instead that “the fact is that people who arrive here on small boats are not illegal migrants. They are people who are seeking asylum.”

His intervention came as residents of the Suffolk village of Barnham voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

Approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday. There were 257 votes for independence, 16 against and one spoiled ballot.

After the vote, Helen Beck, the chair of Barnham Residents’ Association, said Barnham’s flag would be a stone-curlew on a “Suffolk blue background”.

RAF Barnham was one of three Ministry of Defence sites named in June by the government as potential locations for new developments to house asylum seekers.

A similar referendum was held in Piddington, Oxfordshire in September, with residents also voting to leave the UK amid plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at another former military base.

In Barnham, the plans have prompted protests outside the site. The referendum asked residents whether they supported seeking a “crown dependency status”, which is a similar system to that of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man.

John Bauer, the parish council chair, said this would allow the village to “retain loyalty to the crown” but remove itself from Home Office jurisdiction.

While in opposition the Labour party had attacked the Conservative policy to house asylum seekers on military bases; once in government, however, the party backtracked. The Conservatives have also reversed their position, with Kemi Badenoch telling frustrated villagers “the Conservative party is on your side”.

“We know that the problem of the boats needs to stop and we have got a plan to stop it,” she said on Friday.

Earlier this month, it was announced construction company Kier would design the new camp at RAF Barnham.

Before Saturday’s vote Labour’s Dr Peter Prinsley, the local MP, said he was against the development of the site. Prinsley said the plans resembled a “concentration camp”, and warned that planning permission may be difficult to attain due to environmental concerns about rare species living in the area – in particular, stone-curlews – with previous development applications nearby having been turned down.

“This is a symbolic referendum,” Prinsley said. “It’s not going to produce a binding result. I’m expecting that [the result] will be hugely in favour of becoming a crown dependency. There are 500 electors, so I’m expecting it to be 500 – nil.”

He added that the government “is doing an awful lot to deal with the irregular migration problem”, and highlighted that net migration may come down to “more or less zero by the end of the year”.

But he added that he didn’t think “the large army camps in remote locations are ever likely to be appropriate for the distribution of people seeking asylum. The fact is that people who arrive here on small boats are not illegal migrants. They are people who are seeking asylum. Our political opponents have described these people as ‘illegals, criminals, rapists’, and all sorts of things that they’re not. They’re just people who have arrived on small boats. The government is getting a grip on this problem, but it’s a complicated problem.”

He said the proposed Barnham site had particular issues which may make it unsuitable. “It’s a remote location without any pedestrian access, it’s on a very hazardous main road. When it was used as military accommodation there were serious accidents on that road.

“It’s also a site of special scientific interest because it is the nesting site for stone-curlews, which will make any planning application very difficult – even a government planning application – because these are worldwide protections.”

He suggested “disused office blocks in some of the larger cities” may be more appropriate places to house asylum seekers, with more local services available.

“It feels like a concentration camp,” Prinsley added. “It doesn’t feel like a place that has a compassionate approach to people who are fleeing persecution and are being processed for asylum.”

He also said legitimate criticism of the plans had been co-opted by opposition parties who are aiming to “stir up racial discord”.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

“The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

“This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.”
output.standfirst: Dr Peter Prinsley rejected claims that migrants are “illegals, criminals, rapists” after Barnham residents voted 257 to 16 for symbolic independence in protest at plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a former RAF base, which he likened to a “concentration camp”.
output.progress: Prinsley is pushing for the plan to be sited in cities instead, and environmental protections for the base's nesting stone-curlews may yet block it.

output.headline: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck celebrated for 'epoch-defining' satire
output.bodyHtml:
Peter Fluck, the cartoonist and puppeteer who co-created the satirical television show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

“The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch-defining,” a family statement said.

Spitting Image ran for 12 years from 1984 and featured puppet caricatures of politicians, royals and celebrities, including Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth.

Fluck’s family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall after a recent illness, the BBC reported.

Fluck developed the pioneering comedy show with his former college friend Roger Law.

“With Roger Law (‘Luck and Flaw’), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image,” his family added.

“Peter’s creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention.”

Central Independent Television commissioned the first series of Spitting Image for ITV in 1984, and the show ran for 18 seasons, achieving ratings of about 18 million viewers at its highest point.

Thatcher was depicted as an aggressive “iron lady”-type figure while David Steel, then leader of the Liberal party, was caricatured as the weak sidekick of David Owen, the former foreign secretary in James Callaghan’s government.

Fluck told the Guardian in an interview in 2014 how he transitioned from drawing to making Spitting Image.

The caricaturist, who was born in Cambridge in 1941, said: “Roger Law and I used to make a living drawing caricatures for the press. But when Murdoch started buying up Fleet Street, the illustrators and caricaturists were booted out for well-written pieces by intelligent journalists.

“Fortunately, someone had the bright idea that the 2D work we’d been doing on the page could be made into puppets. Sure, we thought, not realising we’d have to make the bloody things.

“We’d start with photographs, then create a caricature that would get modelled in clay. You couldn’t have a 16ft-long nose: it’s impractical in a TV studio.

“A mould of the head was then made, and from that came a foam rubber skin the puppeteer could put on their hand. The puppets were all lifesize – clothes are far cheaper from Oxfam than a wardrobe department.

“The studios were in Birmingham, but the puppets were made on the East India Docks in London. Every Saturday, a lorry would be filled with puppets and driven up the M1.

“I used to have dreams about the back door opening, and all these heads falling into the fast lane.”

In the opening episode, the royal family sketches were cut at the last minute “as a matter of courtesy” to the Duke of Edinburgh, who was opening Central’s new Nottingham studios a few days later, the Times reported.

The duke later appeared in the programme in naval uniform making distasteful remarks about foreign cultures, while Queen Elizabeth was a motherly figure who would “never go to the toilet because I’m queen”.

King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, was depicted as someone who preferred talking to his plants rather than his wife while becoming increasingly irate with the wait to accede to the throne.

Fluck said in 2014: “A wonderful thing was the small amount of really vicious hate mail that would come in on Monday morning. We also had a lot of abuse from the red tops, saying how dare we criticise the royal family. It would have been rather regrettable if we hadn’t.”

An ITV spokesperson said: “Peter Fluck’s creative contribution to TV satire is simply unrivalled; in co-creating Spitting Image, which ran for 18 series in its original incarnation, his cutting edge puppetry and caricature skills, alongside the show’s sharp and always shrewdly observed humour, became a defining part of the cultural zeitgeist. Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his family and friends at this very sad time.”
output.standfirst: Peter Fluck, who with Roger Law invented the latex puppet caricatures of politicians and royals that powered Spitting Image for 12 years, has died aged 85 after a recent illness, at home in Cornwall.

output.headline: England crush All Blacks for record win, inspired by Lewis Moody's return
output.bodyHtml:
Every year the All Blacks come to south-west London it feels like an acid test. And rarely, if ever, have England responded with such class and conviction on this famous old stretch of grass. New Zealand simply could not live with their clear-eyed, motivated opponents who, at times, made their illustrious visitors look horribly second-rate.

If Kiwi fans thought last week’s loss to Wales was painful this was arguably as bad in terms of the reputational damage. The home side were 19-0 up after 36 minutes and had the game all but wrapped up within a couple of minutes of the restart when Ollie Chessum smashed his way over to claim his side’s fourth try. In terms of England’s margin of victory, this was New Zealand’s heaviest loss to any northern hemisphere nation in their proud history.

Related: England hail ‘inspirational’ Moody after thrashing New Zealand

There were even occasions when the fabled silver fern was in danger of being utterly trampled, with almost three-quarters of the game taking place in the New Zealand half. If anything it was England who more closely resembled the slick All Black sides of yesteryear, particularly in the first half when tries from Henry Slade, Jack van Poortvliet and Ben Earl rewarded the hosts’ purposeful approach play, set-piece accuracy and seemingly greater desire.

The significant improvement in their backline fluency is certainly a tribute to, among others, their attack coach, Lee Blackett, but, best of all, England are finally emerging as the all-court team they aspire to be. Their captain, Maro Itoje, had teed this up as “a massive game” in terms of “showing the world where we believe this team can go” and that lofty objective was gloriously achieved despite the pre-game injury withdrawal of the winger Tommy Freeman.

Related: England’s strength in depth finally comes together in landmark All Blacks victory | Andy Bull

The bench also left an impression, as did the sight of England’s former captain Lewis Moody lining up with the current players as they faced the haka. Initially Moody, now an inspiring campaigner for motor neurone research, stood up front before the England team moved in front of him and, in some cases, even entered into the All Black half. As a symbol of intent it was also as powerful as any seen on this ground down the years.

The huge emotional impact, however, had to be balanced against the loss of Freeman with a thigh problem, less than ideal with their other prolific wing, Manny Feyi-Waboso, already sidelined. Cadan Murley stepped up to start on the left wing with Will Joseph switching to the right but England’s sense of purpose was never remotely diluted. As early as the fifth minute they had their first try on the board after Fin Smith spotted some space in behind and Slade was quickest to react to his fly-half’s perfectly weighted grubber kick.

Itoje and his head coach, Steve Borthwick, had both been urging their team to make a fast start and their instructions had clearly not fallen on deaf ears. New Zealand also fell foul of the Australian referee Nic Berry at the breakdown from an early stage and fumbled their lines even when they did make it into the home 22.

England, by contrast, forced their way into the All Black 22 five times inside the first 25 minutes. New Zealand, though, appeared to have picked up one or two lessons from Wales’s heroic goalline stand in Cardiff and initially repeatedly kept them out, most notably when Alex Coles was held up. There was another frustrating false start when Smith kicked the ball dead from a scrum penalty that should have put New Zealand right back into coffin corner.

Could England be in danger of blowing all their good work? Happily for their supporters the answer was to be a resounding “no”. With the All Blacks again under siege close to their own line after another lovely attack by Slade, the slight figure of Van Poortvliet swallow-dived over to score his side’s second try. Then came the defining moment of the half. Earl is an excellent athlete but to watch him blast through the lone tackle of Cam Roigard and storm to the line would have been painful viewing for Tonbridge under-11s, never mind New Zealand.

Ethan de Groot did grab a try back two minutes before the interval but the half-time horror for Kiwis watching aghast through their fingers back at home was about to get even worse. England once again made yards down the middle before moving the ball wide and, not for the first time, there was Chessum to hammer home the final nail in the left corner.

Related: Fading Beauden Barrett a symbol of rabble All Blacks’ joyless decline | Gerard Meagher

It was certainly no way for Beauden Barrett to celebrate his 150th cap, even if the great man did score a smart trademark try from a nice Roigard offload. Otherwise Dave Rennie, a good rugby man suddenly caught in the headlamps of an onrushing locomotive, had very little to console him as England’s replacements maintained the suffocating pressure.

Maybe England could have even eclipsed the 38 points they scored against these same opponents in 2012 when Manu Tuilagi was running amok. They ultimately had to settle for a 62nd minute try scored by the quietly impressive Seb Atkinson, another player whose stock is now rising rapidly. Finals weekend, for the moment, can wait.
output.standfirst:
• England beat New Zealand 37-12, their heaviest-ever defeat to a northern hemisphere side

  • Former captain Lewis Moody, who has motor neurone disease, joined the haka
output.progress: Players say former captain Lewis Moody, who has motor neurone disease, helped inspire their performance by joining the pre-match haka.

output.headline: British father recalls the moment his two-year-old son fell to his death in Cyprus
output.bodyHtml:
A British father has recalled the moment his two-year-old son slipped from his grasp and fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus, for which he was later fined by the courts.

Joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Prosecutors in Cyprus had refused to drop the case against him.

During recent court proceedings, it was heard that Foster thought the window at the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas was closed when he approached it with his son, Jaxon, to show him the view of a waterpark.

The 37-year-old “lost control” of him, the Paphos district court was told, before the boy fell 10 metres (33ft). The fall happened on 12 July, the first day of the Fosters’ family holiday.

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Foster said: “I have a burden. I’ll have that my whole life. It’s very traumatic. My mind doesn’t want to go there. I just remember the despair of him falling, and watching him fall.

“It was just such a shock … I put him up thinking he was going against a glass pane … and then he wasn’t there.”

The toddler was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after he suffered severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.

Foster recalled his outpouring of emotion when he located his son after the fall. “I picked him up. I held him and screamed,” he said. The Essex-born auditor said he and his wife had an hour with their son’s body after he was pronounced dead.

The decision to charge Foster, reported to be a senior accountant at KPMG, was criticised by his legal representatives, as well as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats, who said it lacked compassion.

The charge Foster accepted is usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents. It carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison, but the fine he was handed was the lightest sentence possible for the offence.

At his sentencing in October, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, describing the incident as a “tragic event”.

The court had heard that, while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood, it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.

Foster was detained after the fall. He reportedly had to tell his eldest child, a daughter, about her brother’s death via a video call while he was being held.

He posted €30,000 (£26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the funeral of his son in August, but was required, under threat of extradition, to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.

In a push for clemency, Foster’s legal team had appealed in September to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds. The request was denied.

Since returning home, Foster said the focus of his grieving family has turned to their daughter.

“It’s very difficult,” he said. “She waves at the sky and says: ‘I love you’ to him and blows a kiss. She’s lost her best friend. She’s gone from having a sibling to being an only child.”
output.standfirst: Joshua Foster was fined after his son Jaxon fell from a hotel window on the family's first day in Cyprus; his young daughter now blows kisses to the sky for her brother

output.headline: 14-month investigation cracks alleged $22m California rail heist ring
output.bodyHtml:
Fourteen people in southern California have been accused of burglarizing more than $22m worth of goods from moving freight trains, in a plot reminiscent of the US old west, when outlaws and bandits wreaked havoc on the nascent railroad industry.

The justice department has brought railroad theft charges against the group for raiding at least 36 trains and selling thousands of stolen Nike sneakers, among other products, on the black market.

“The scale of the theft is staggering,” first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said.

Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, was the alleged ringleader for the so-called “Los Trenes” (“the trains”) scheme, which spanned 2024 through 2026. Court documents did not list an attorney for Angel or the other charged individuals.

Each robbery took a similar form.

Angel’s associates, including his father and two uncles, stowed away on moving freight trains, according to a grand jury indictment.

With some of the men on board serving as lookouts, the others would slash the train’s air hose, causing a sudden loss of air pressure and forcing an emergency stop of the entire vehicle. The maneuver is perilous given the risks of derailment.

Once the train was disabled, the rest of the Los Trenes crew would swoop in to load up the stolen goods and stash the loot at houses across southern California, prosecutors say.

Angel posed for a selfie, where he threw up the peace sign, in front of several boxes containing Nike merchandise, in a February 2024 photograph, attached to court documents.

The next burglary would come months later.

In October 2024, Donta Hedgeman, 27, sawed through the lock of a container on a moving Nike train, according to video evidence.

The heists ramped up in 2025, even as signs emerged that law enforcement was catching on to the alleged thefts.

An unidentified “co-conspirator” texted 23-year-old Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez on 17 April 2025 to say he had been arrested for receiving stolen property.

“They want me to tell them who did I get them from and who had the other pairs,” the person wrote.

Martinez responded, instructing the person to contact him over Signal, an app with encrypted messaging.

Twelve days later, the crew made off with 1,170 tools and 17,000 parts from Milwaukee Tool.

Police officers appeared to sniff around an unnamed company, which purchased a slew of stolen products from the crew in the fall of 2025.

A different “co-conspirator” speculated on their fate. “Good luck with them wires/if they go deep in the case/You’re cooked,” they wrote to Martinez.

Then, on 16 January 2026, Angel and 25-year-old Fredy Marquina referenced a partner being intercepted by police: “They just got Jorge for buying and receiving/stolen property.”

Once again, faced with the mounting risk of being caught, the men proceeded with further heists in the summer of 2026.

In July 2026, Angel Sanchez, 24, shared an AI-generated image that appeared to glamorize their robbery spree.

Masked men tossed Nike sneakers off a Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway (BNSR) train into luxury cars inscribed with the words “Los Trenes”.

In the image, a helicopter circled above, shining a searchlight.

If convicted of the conspiracy charge, the men face at least five years in prison. The theft of interstate railroad charge has a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.

A conviction for violence against railroad carriers would carry the most severe punishment with a possibility of life in prison.

Prosecutors described this week’s sweeping indictment as the culmination of a 14-month-long investigation.

“We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market,” said Nathan Hochman, the Los Angeles county district attorney.
output.standfirst: US prosecutors have charged 14 people with forcing freight trains to emergency stops by slashing air hoses, a manoeuvre that risked derailment, then stealing more than $22m in goods including Nike trainers and tools.
output.progress: The justice department says its 14-month investigation has led to charges carrying significant prison time for the alleged ringleaders.

output.headline: Borthwick's England finally click as depth delivers record win over All Blacks
output.trail: A record-breaking win over New Zealand suggests Steve Borthwick's side are realising their enormous potential at last.

output.headline: All Blacks coach calls for reaction against England after Wales defeat
output.trail: Dave Rennie, the New Zealand head coach, said the team 'let ourselves down and let our country down' in Cardiff and called for 'a reaction' against England at Twickenham.

output.headline: England eye rare twin Twickenham scalps as All Blacks regroup
output.trail: After their seismic defeat by Wales, New Zealand face the prospect of history repeating itself in unwanted ways.

output.headline: England told to play with freedom against cornered All Blacks
output.trail: New Zealand want to ease the pain of their defeat by Wales, but England's squad depth makes them formidable opponents.

output.headline: Itoje says discipline and bench impact will decide 'massive' Twickenham test
output.trail: England and New Zealand meet with final Nations Championship spots and reputations on the line.

output.headline: Five-try form earns Will Joseph another chance to start for England
output.trail: Joseph is poised to be rewarded for his five-try performance against Japan with another England start, against New Zealand on Saturday.

output.headline: F1 teams adapt with last-minute travel changes to reach Melbourne
output.trail: As many as a thousand members of the Formula One circus were forced into last-minute travel changes to reach Melbourne's opening round amid the Middle East conflict.

output.headline: Russell claims pole ahead of Antonelli as Norris qualifies sixth in Melbourne
output.trail: George Russell edged Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli to claim pole for the Australian Grand Prix, while world champion Lando Norris qualified sixth.

output.headline: Piastri apologises to home fans after crashing out before Australian GP begins
output.trail: The McLaren driver said 'I'm just very sorry' after a mishap during the formation lap at Albert Park ended his home race before it began.

output.headline: Lewis Hamilton denies lack of trust at 'super united' Ferrari before Las Vegas GP
output.trail: The British driver says the F1 team is 'working on our communication', after he held clear-the-air talks with teammate Charles Leclerc.

output.headline: Lando Norris wins sprint race at F1 Miami Grand Prix as McLaren roar back
output.trail: Norris won the sprint race at the Miami Grand Prix with a dominant drive for McLaren, beating teammate Oscar Piastri into second.

output.headline: British man, 22, dies in Cyprus knife attack after public urination dispute
output.trail: George Low, 22, was stabbed to death and his friend was wounded in a knife attack on a Sunday in Ayia Napa, following a dispute over a claim of urinating in public.

output.headline: British cousins extradited to Cyprus over death of motorcyclist
output.trail: Michael Binnington and Luke Atkinson flew to Nicosia to serve three-year terms despite legal concerns.

output.headline: British teenager leaves Cyprus after being told she is free to go
output.trail: The 19-year-old was seen at Larnaca airport hours after being told she was free to leave the country, following the Cyprus rape case.

output.headline: Cyprus foreign minister calls for 'conversation' on future of UK bases
output.trail: The call follows a drone strike that hit RAF Akrotiri without being detected in time, raising doubts about the island's British bases.

output.headline: Cyprus will allow vaccinated British tourists from 1 May
output.trail: Visitors will need a vaccine approved by the EMA, administered at least seven days before travel.

output.headline: Cyprus affirms its neutrality as a 'pillar of peace' amid regional tensions
output.trail: Officials expressed shock after Hezbollah named Cyprus as a potential target over the Israel war, but stressed the country's neutral, peaceful stance.

output.headline: Mediator to decide whether Nick Reiner can use trust fund for murder defence
output.trail: The son of Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, who is accused of killing his parents, says the funds have been withheld.

output.headline: Thirty district attorneys challenge Newsom's mass clemency for condemned inmates
output.trail: The lawsuit, filed on behalf of victims' families and advocates, seeks to stop Gavin Newsom's commutation of death sentences in California.

output.headline: Newsom commutes more than 500 death sentences in California
output.trail: The Democrat's move prevents these people from being executed under future governors, after Christa Pike's failed execution.

output.headline: Baby with rare heart defect at centre of surrogacy case in critical condition
output.trail: The biological parents have secured a restraining order against the surrogate as the lawsuit continues and the baby receives care.

output.headline: 'Regain your humanity': jailed anti-AI protester's message to OpenAI and Meta
output.trail: Wynd Kaufmyn, 69 — the first anti-AI protester to be jailed — chained and locked the doors of OpenAI's headquarters last year with fellow StopAI members.

output.headline: Patricia Krenwinkel, former Manson follower, granted parole after nearly six decades
output.trail: The 78-year-old has spent nearly six decades in prison; California's governor had overturned her last two parole grants.

output.headline: Pancreatic cancer pill marks 'biggest breakthrough in decades', trial shows
output.trail: In the daraxonrasib trial, cancer became undetectable in one in 12 patients, while tumours stopped growing in nearly all participants.

output.headline: BepiColombo becomes only the second spacecraft ever to orbit Mercury
output.trail: The double probe will map the planet's surface and study its interior to shed light on its unusually large core.

output.headline: Cyber defenders head off attack on UK supermarket fridges and freezers
output.trail: News of the vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries were hit by cyber-attacks.

output.headline: New England fishers find a 'godsend' in offshore wind, despite Trump
output.trail: Despite the president's attacks on the industry, Sea Services is training fishers in offshore wind construction and giving them a second income stream.

output.headline: Anthropic's record-breaking stock market debut raises billions for AI lab
output.trail: The historic IPO raised billions for the AI frontier lab, though experts say the coming months could prove bumpy as the industry faces a variety of challenges.
